title: Farage and Tice sue NCA over alleged leaks of financial information
description: Richard Tice has said he and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage are suing the National Crime Agency (NCA) over the alleged leaking of confidential financia
body: Richard Tice has said he and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage are suing the National Crime Agency (NCA) over the alleged leaking of confidential financial information.The Boston and Skegness MP and Reform deputy leader told Talk TV they believed the NCA had committed "multiple criminal offences" and said they would be seeking an apology and damages.He accused them of leaking "individual bank statements, bank transfers, details of conversations with bank managers from different banks".Last month Tice wrote to the agency to ask if they would investigate whether they were responsible for the leaking of private financial information to the media.It followed reports that payments made to his company Britain Means Business by the mother of the convicted fraudster George Cottrell were flagged to the NCA as part of its suspicious activity reports (SARs) programme, which alerts law enforcement to potential instances of money laundering.SARs are not crime reports.Tice said at the time he only became aware of it when contacted by the Guardian newspaper, which broke the story.The NCA has been carrying out an internal investigation but Tice told Talk TV it was "playing for time and we've said we're done with it".A Reform UK spokesperson said claims had been filed at the High Court. BBC News has not seen the detail of the claims.A spokesperson for the NCA said: "Following complaints brought by Richard Tice MP and Nigel Farage, the NCA's Professional Standards Unit is conducting an investigation. That work is ongoing. It would not be appropriate to comment further at this time."As first reported by the Telegraph, Tice's company Tisun Investment received a loan of £80,000 from Cottrell in late 2024.That same year, Britain Means Business received a £1m donation from Cotrell's mother.Data from the Electoral Commission shows that Britain Means Business donated £500,000 to Reform UK in the same month.These payments were flagged to the NCA as part of the SARs programme.Cottrell's relationship with Reform has been under scrutiny in recent months after the Sunday Times reported he had supplied Farage with support including security and social media staff in the year before he became an MP.Under parliamentary rules, newly elected MPs have to declare gifts or benefits received in the 12 months before their election that relate to their "parliamentary or political activities".However, there is an exemption for gifts and benefits that are "purely personal".Reform has argued that Farage did not breach the guidelines by not declaring the support from Cottrell because the support was provided in a "purely personal capacity".

schema.headline: Farage and Tice sue NCA over alleged leaks of financial information

title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'
description: Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on t
body: Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention – "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.He's right – digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18–30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera."I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids – where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image – are also popular on socials right now.With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time."If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman. "Phone photos have warped our perception of time."It's not just digital cameras returning from the archives (or a dusty cupboard), but early MP3 devices like iPods too.According to refurbished tech website Backmarket, iPods are "driving the trend" in sales of older MP3 devices with a 48% increase in sales between 2024 and 2025, with demand for MP3 and MP4 players "accelerating further into 2026".Cheri Sanih, 30, runs a Tumblr account about older technology which she says has gained thousands of followers recently.As she scrolls through the music library on her mint green iPod, filled with album artwork from 15 to 20 years ago, childhood memories of receiving one as a Christmas present come flooding back.For her, it's all about nostalgically "wanting to remember simpler times"; being able to "bury into escapism".Sanih points out how her "phone is always getting notifications and sometimes I just want to be outside, blissfully listening to music".She thinks iPods have become popular again because of their "beautiful design" and the way the music player is "the first bit of technology really catering to humans with a less cluttered user interface".And speaking of back to basics, wired headphones are perhaps as simple as you can get, but again proving popular online.These are now a daily staple for 23-year-old Monique Wellman-Mason from Bristol, who grew tired of losing her wireless earbuds."Every single time I get them out my bag I spend two minutes trying to detangle them which is a bit of a pain," she jokes, "but at the same time I love that they have a microphone and I'm [always] connected to my phone".She tells the BBC that the clear mic is useful for her job as a social media manager and she enjoys being able to "spark that nostalgia", while another positive is wired earphones are "really cheap" at about £20.Monique made the switch from bluetooth wireless to wired earphones a few months back and says she hasn't returned to the former since. "Technology only goes up and we're always looking for the quickest thing but this is a step back in a way – I love it," she says.Whether it's digital cameras, iPods or wired earphones, does a renewed love for early-digital gadgets among some young people tell us something more?It's been on the mind of Andrew Przybylski, professor of technology and human behaviour at the University of Oxford.Underpinning a fondness for more basic tech is "people's desire on a very deep level to be in control of their experiences," he argues.He says the modern digital world often leaves us inflicted by decision paralysis, external - the inability to choose because there are so many options.When a new series comes out, he explains, "binge watching it automatically" often feels like a decision that is made for us.In contrast, when you choose to turn on a digital camera and play with its settings or add an album to your iPod library "you move towards something you want versus it coming at you".Andrew says "people want more than to just rent the things [and experiences] they're passionate about" and that buying your own music or taking your own pictures creates a sense of connection.He references Xbox's server outage in late July, in which users couldn't play games even if they owned the discs and how "nobody liked that"."Imagine if a book worked that way," he adds.Additional reporting by Amy Walker.

schema.headline: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'

title: 'Sex predator let out to kill' and 'net zero plans rolled back'
description: Several front pages carry pictures of the killer and rapist, Simon Levy, and the women he murdered. The Daily Express says he's "likely to die behind
body: Several front pages carry pictures of the killer and rapist, Simon Levy, and the women he murdered. The Daily Express says he's "likely to die behind bars", external following his conviction yesterday. The Daily Mail describes him as a "Tube Monster", referencing his attacks on the London Underground network. In an article for the paper, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch calls Levy a "modern-day Jack the Ripper", external, and argues a tougher criminal justice system is needed to protect people.The Daily Telegraph says Andy Burnham is considering an "about turn" on blocking the early prison release of two of PC Andrew Harper's killers, external. The Sun quotes a government source as saying the PM is prepared to "explore every option"., externalThe new energy secretary has told the Times that the government could relax some of Labour's net zero targets, external to help reduce the cost of living. Miatta Fahnbulleh tells the paper that ministers won't stick rigidly to a pledge to nearly eliminate fossil fuels from Britain's power supplies by 2030 – if doing so would risk higher household bills.According to the Daily Telegraph, European football's governing body paid off a member of staff – who it claims was an alleged mistress of Gianni Infantino – when he was Uefa's general secretary., external The organisation he now leads, Fifa, tells the paper that Infantino strongly denies the allegations, and that there have never been any complaints by employees about his behaviour. The Telegraph said Uefa had admitted a payment had been made, which it said had been in accordance with regulations at the time, and that those rules had since been tightened.The Guardian casts doubt on the stereotype that holidaying Germans hog sun loungers. It highlights a poll of European tourists by YouGov, that suggests the Italians and the French are more likely to reserve a spot with a towel, external. According to the paper, the British are the least likely to hog a sun lounger.

schema.headline: 'Sex predator let out to kill' and 'net zero plans rolled back'

title: Hunter Biden says pardon was 'not good' for America or his father's legacy
description: Hunter Biden has told the BBC he is "the most privileged person there is" after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President J
body: Hunter Biden has told the BBC he is "the most privileged person there is" after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President Joe Biden, acknowledging it was not a good choice for America or his father's legacy. In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC's Newsnight, Hunter Biden defended the controversial pardon, revealed his father's "painful" cancer has spread, ruled out seeking elected office and spoke about helping others recover from addiction.Asked about the 2024 pardon, he said he understood the criticism but noted: "What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me.""It's something that is easily criticised and for good reason," he added."It's not fair… All I know is that I'm grateful that he did it for me," he said, acknowledging the pardon was "not good" for the American people, the Constitution - or his father's legacy. He argued to the BBC that his father ultimately acted out of concern that he would become a target under Donald Trump's incoming administration."I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father."Hunter Biden also insisted he and his father had never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted."There is no way that you can have those kinds of discussions that would not become public," he said.President Biden granted his son a full and unconditional pardon in December 2024, despite repeatedly saying beforehand that he would not use the powers of the presidency to intervene in his son's legal cases. In announcing the decision, the former president said his son had been "selectively and unfairly prosecuted".The pardon covered his son's federal gun conviction, a tax case he'd pled guilty to and any federal offences committed between 2014 and 2024. Asked about the depths of his addiction, he described drinking almost a gallon of vodka a day while smoking crack cocaine almost every 15 minutes at its worst. "It was hell on earth," he said. "There's nothing glamorous about it."Reflecting on why he turned to drugs and alcohol, Hunter Biden rejected the suggestion that he felt untouchable because he was the son of a president."I wasn't reaching for anything except oblivion," he said. He noted that his addiction was a way to escape feelings of anxiety and isolation. The drugs and alcohol initially felt like a solution before becoming "the thing that almost killed me", he noted. Hunter Biden got emotional at times in the interview, notably when discussing his father's health. Cancer is really hard," he said, stopping to clear his throat. "It's really sad to watch."He revealed that the "cancer has spread, metastasised into his bones and further. It's very painful" and "very debilitating". "My dad is, to this day, the centre of our family," he said. "He's the best father, the best husband, the best grandfather.""The only thing that I say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more."Hunter Biden also reflected on the presidential debate in June 2024 that ultimately ended his father's re-election campaign. He said he had watched it from his home in California and immediately sensed something was wrong."I was shocked," he said. "I knew something was wrong."

schema.headline: Hunter Biden says pardon was 'not good' for America or his father's legacy

title: Child among three dead in Russian nightly strikes near Kyiv
description: At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, a local official said.In the
body: At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, a local official said.In the early hours of Saturday missiles hit east of the capital and witnesses reported hearing powerful explosions just days after strikes across Ukraine killed 21 people.The ballistic missile strikes killed three and wounded another three, the head of the regional military administration Timur Tkachenko said, adding that falling debris damaged apartment buildings and cars, while a fire broke out at a separate building.Emergency crews were also fighting fires at a building and fuel tank in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaly Klitchko wrote on Telegram.Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS shared photos showing garages, a business and a building on fire in Kyiv, adding: "The number of victims is being clarified."President Volodymyr Zelensky has arrived in the Serbian capital Belgrade for his first visit. He is due to meet with Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić to discuss economic ties, security issues and relations with the European Union.

schema.headline: Child among three dead in Russian nightly strikes near Kyiv

title: Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue
description: Image source, Kiama CouncilImage caption, A former apprentice stonemason who helped build the Houses of Parliament is thought to have borrowed the boo
body: Image source, Kiama CouncilImage caption, A former apprentice stonemason who helped build the Houses of Parliament is thought to have borrowed the book in the late 1800sByLana LamSydneyA book borrowed 150 years ago has finally been returned to an Australian library, with the culprit linked to the Houses of Parliament in London.Antiquities of Athens was borrowed from a local library in Kiama, a seaside town about 120km (75 miles) south of Sydney, some time in the mid-1870s.The book on classic Greek architecture was stored in a tea chest hidden behind a boarded-up fireplace for decades before it was recently discovered by a family member.Ross Simmons, 77, thinks his great-grandfather, John Simmons, might have borrowed the book to help with his career, having worked as an apprentice stonemason in Westminster in the mid-1800s before becoming an architect in Australia.Image source, Kiama CouncilImage caption, The book was a little water damaged but otherwise in a good conditionSimmons, a self-confessed family history buff, said his great-grandfather studied in London between 1839 to 1844."After his studies in London, he was apprenticed to other stonemasons to help in the construction of the Houses of Parliament," Simmons said.In 1857, aged 27, John Simmons emigrated from the UK to Australia, first living in the Sydney suburb of Newtown before relocating to Kiama after leading the construction of a sandstone church in the coastal town."He had quite an interest in architecture, construction and building," Simmons said, adding that the overdue book "probably sat on a shelf at his house" and was used as a reference.The book somehow ended up in a tea chest - along with other family records - which was placed in a fireplace that was covered up.Image source, Supplied: Jo HartmannImage caption, The fireplace where the book was found had been sealed for decadesAbout 30 years ago, the tea chest was uncovered during renovations and the books - including the overdue one - were given to Simmons for safekeeping.But it wasn't until about a fortnight ago that he went through some of the books in greater detail."I looked inside the front cover and, lo and behold, on the second page there was a Kiama Library stamp," Simmons said, with the library's borrowing conditions also detailed on the inside cover.For instance, library members could only borrow one book at a time, unless it could be proved that six people in the same household could read, in which case, three books could be lent out.Anyone intoxicated was barred from borrowing and members returning books past their due date would be fined three pence for every week it was late.Kiama Library staff worked out that the fine would be £97 - or in today's currency  AU$28,000 ($20,000; £15,000), allowing for inflation. But luckily for the Simmons family, the fine has been waived.Kiama Council libraries manager Michelle Hudson said the unusual find had attracted a lot of attention.Image source, Jane ThompsonImage caption, Kiama Council libraries manager Michelle Hudson said people have travelled from out of town to come and see the book"People have travelled 40 minutes away to come and actually hold the book... it's a beautiful little book and it's got an amazing story to tell," she said.The cloth-bound volume has some water damage but otherwise, is in good condition, Hudson said."It does have beautiful illustrations in it and some pages that fold out to show you they were using exact measurements of some of the monuments in Greece."She said in 1872, the council got a £200 grant to establish the town's library and and it had fewer than 1,000 books in its collection, with the overdue book marked as number 506.Image source, Catherine TaylorImage caption, The book, published in 1858, features Greek monument illustrations that fold outThere's no way to know exactly who borrowed the book or when, Hudson said, as the library's borrowing records from that period have since been lost.However, the book is no longer available to borrow, having been added to the library's collection of special items, which can be viewed on request. "It won't be able to go out again... we don't want to wait another 150 years for it to come back," Hudson joked.As for the book's much-delayed return, Simmons said he believes his great-grandfather would be pleased with the final chapter of its journey."I think he'd be happy to see the book returned and he'd probably have a bit of a laugh about it."Image source, Kiama LibraryImage caption, The book was borrowed from the library which was housed in this building from 1872 to 1890

schema.headline: Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue

title: Appeals court halts Trump's ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown
description: "Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People's
body: "Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People's ​House — to fit a particular President's desires," the panel said.The three-judge panel, in a 2-1 decision, said: "Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence.""The President has no - and claims no - constitutionally assigned authority over that property, which is designed and maintained for the use of all Presidents, current and future, and for the American people," the opinion said.The administration appealed to the court after a federal judge twice blocked above-ground construction on the ballroom, while still allowing underground work to proceed.The ruling on Friday upholds the order blocking above-ground construction without congressional approval. The appeals court delayed implementation of its ruling for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal to the Supreme Court.The BBC has contacted the White House and Department of Justice for comment. Trump railed against the "horrendous" and "politically motivated" decision on social media, highlighting the dissenting judge's opinion that the order is "a blatant abuse of discretion".He said the military and Secret Service viewed the ruling as a national security threat."This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety," he wrote.He also repeated that the ballroom was being built ahead of schedule and under budget, as a gift to the American people funded by a coalition of private donors.However, Republicans have sought to use a portion of $1bn (£740m) in taxpayer funds for Secret Service security upgrades - a plan that was brushed aside by a budget watchdog in May.President Trump has asserted that the new ballroom is needed to "accommodate people for grand parties, State Visits", and has also said that it is "vital for National Security".The ballroom building would consist of the large entertaining space above ground and also a security complex below ground. Trump doubled down on the need for the space after an assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in April.The National Trust for Historic Preservation celebrated the ruling on Friday, noting that no above-ground construction can take place "unless and until" Congress takes action."The White House, a global landmark that symbolizes American identity and the ideals of democracy, belongs to the American people," said Brent Leggs, President and CEO of the National Trust."The National Trust for Historic Preservation and its partners are proud to defend this irreplaceable monument on behalf of all Americans."Trump has touted the ballroom project repeatedly since he unveiled plans for it in July 2025. It would have been the most substantial structural change to the presidential residence in more than 70 years.But the project has been mired in legal issues since October, when the Trump administration demolished the East Wing, which was built in 1902, to begin construction. Trump initially said the project would be "near" the East Wing, not that it would be demolished.Government lawyers have argued the additional security complex and features included in the ballroom project are needed to protect the White House complex from drones, ballistic missiles, biohazards and other threats - changes essential to protecting the president, his family, and staff. Trump said on Friday that construction includes bomb shelters, hospital and medical facilities and top secret military facilities. But the Trust said there was no basis to "disturb" the White House and argued that having a ballroom isn't a national security emergency.The three-judge appeals court panel said on Friday that its ruling "has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable", nor does it weigh in on whether the administration may ultimately construct the ballroom. "What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require," the order said.

schema.headline: Appeals court halts Trump's ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown

title: Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover'
description: Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegr
body: Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation, external.A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming "a departure payment was made to the individual in question".The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment.The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body."Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph."No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school. It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and "reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation".

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover'

title: Full body MOTs - the future of healthcare or a headache for the NHS?
description: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shockImage source, BBC and Neko HealthImage caption, More than 2,000 images were taken of Ruth's
body: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shockImage source, BBC and Neko HealthImage caption, More than 2,000 images were taken of Ruth's skinByRuth CleggHealth and wellbeing reporter I don't mind having my photo taken - triple checked and filtered for Instagram - but 70 cameras pointing at me while I'm down to my knickers is a bit daunting.A robotic voice tells me to stay still and close my eyes as I stand in a huge curved scanner while classical music plays in the background.With a flash of light, 2,000 photographs are taken of my body, in the hope of capturing every mark, freckle and mole to analyse for different skin cancers.This full-body scan is happening at a sci-fi-style clinic in Manchester city centre, with me wearing a dressing gown and hexagon-shaped rubber slippers. The millions of data points collected will create a 3D avatar of my body using AI.Over the past two years, the market for health MOTs has boomed, with people willing to pay hundreds, or even thousands, for them, and companies such as Prenuvo, Ezra and Neko Health raising millions in venture capital. While Prenuvo and Ezra offer a whole-body MRI scan, I've opted for Neko Health, which doesn't delve quite as deeply, and comes with a more modest £299 price tag. There are currently 100,000 people on its waiting list.Image caption, The body scan industry sees this kind of treatment as a new frontier in healthcareI will be screened for a range of different conditions, including skin cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, eye conditions like glaucoma, as well as kidney and blood disorders. I don't have any symptoms, but what if they do find something? More on that later.The body scan industry sees itself as a new frontier in healthcare, preventing disease before it has a chance to fully appear. But there is scepticism about how beneficial these scans really are for otherwise healthy patients. My socials are inundated with videos of enthusiastic clients filming themselves in scan machines, getting their bloods taken and testing their grip strength.Hjalmar Nilsonne, one of the founders of Neko Health, wants to see this preventative treatment available for every individual, not just those who can afford to pay for it."While medicine has progressed so much over the past century, primary care is still very basic. Why wait until we see symptoms?" Nilsonne says. "The data is super clear - prevention is preferable to cure."However, GPs and doctors in the wider NHS are more sceptical, with NHS England warning that the popularity of these scans is leading to more "over-diagnosis, unnecessary investigations and avoidable anxiety".As well as having a scan myself, I've spoken to two women who had very different experiences.'My cancerous skin marks were missed'Image source, AnnabelImage caption, Annabel had four cancerous markings removedAnnabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology."I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions."It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment."Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment."We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".'It saved my life'Image source, MehvishImage caption, Mehvish's long-term blood sugar levels came back very high and she was diagnosed with Latent Autoimmune DiabetesMehvish says nothing could have prepared her for what she was told after her full body scan. She left Birmingham's Neko Health clinic with a life-changing diagnosis."I expected to feel relief," the 33-year-old says. "Instead, I was told that I had a rare form of diabetes."After her long-term blood sugar levels came back very high, she had another blood test which confirmed she had suspected diabetes.She was referred back to her GP, who sent her for an urgent hospital appointment the same day, and was diagnosed with Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA), a type of diabetes which bridges both type 1 and type 2. Like type 1, it is an autoimmune condition that attacks the body's pancreatic cells, but it also shares traits with type 2 because it can progress slowly and, depending on the stage of the condition, it can initially be managed with diet and exercise."I didn't have any of the symptoms," Mehvish says, "It was difficult to get my head round it - how could I have this condition and not know about it?"But she says the early, unexpected intervention "saved my life".Now she injects insulin twice a day, monitors what she eats, and despite missing the spontaneity of her old life, is learning to adapt to her new one."I feel so much better, more clarity, less brain fog and I feel so much more balanced."After my own scan, I'm feeling slightly out of balance. I've been told I have 3,311 skin markings - compared to the average Neko Health client's 845. Three need extra review by the company's dermatologist in Sweden."But I don't have any big moles or markings," I say during the post-scan consultation with a doctor. It's my freckles, I'm told, and having freckles puts me at higher risk of skin cancer.Image source, NEKOImage caption, One of the moles that were flagged as needing extra scrutiny by dermatologists in SwedenHaving felt confident I would get a clean bill of health - especially when it comes to my skin - I was a bit unnerved to discover that I'd need to have extra tests.As well as the three suspicious-looking moles that needed further attention, I also discovered I have an unusual heart rate. The trace from the electrocardiogram (ECG) highlighted an extra wave, known as a bifid P wave, which was referred to Neko Health's in-house cardiologist for review. Thankfully, it came back all clear.A few days later, I received a follow-up text to say there were no abnormal skin changes that required treatment.I am one of thousands of clients who has had something flagged as a potential issue, then later found no further treatment was required. Some doctors say this causes unnecessary anxiety and that patients should only rely on national screening programmes through the NHS. Dr Stephen Harden, president of the Royal Society of Radiologists, points to the technology used in the NHS, which targets "specific areas" like the breasts, bowel or cervix, and which he says may be more reliable than a whole-body scan. But former health minister Steve Brine says precautionary scans like the one I had "fit the direction of travel of how people are approaching their health"."Change is afoot across the NHS - prevention is a huge policy area," Brine says. "We want to identify people's problems before they become patients, so these scans could well become a part of our future healthcare and primary care needs to adapt."As for me? I was told my heart age was four years younger than my actual age, and on the whole, I was in tip-top health. But I've also learned a valuable lesson - that I could be more at risk of skin cancer because of my freckles. So, thanks to my time in the scanner, I am now far more enthusiastic about lathering sunscreen all over my body - rather than only on my face.

schema.headline: Full body MOTs - the future of healthcare or a headache for the NHS?

title: Spain to impose border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies
description: Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies.The measures - which started
body: Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies.The measures - which started at midnight (22:00 GMT) and will last for a month - come a week after Italy introduced similar restrictions following an influx of about 78,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.On Friday, Spain demanded Italy reverse its checks by Sunday. Rome said they would stay until at least 15 August - when, it said, Spain "expects a new wave of migration" to hit Ceuta.The crisis has pitted Spain's socialist leader Pedro Sanchez against Italy's conservative leader Giorgia Meloni - who has long called for stricter EU migration rules.Italy does not share a land border with Spain. Its government said last week that decision to temporarily suspend the ​border-free Schengen arrangement was to prevent any of the migrants who had entered Ceuta from travelling on to Italy.Madrid dismissed this position, saying it was based on "spurious arguments" that lacked any basis in fact because the migrants who entered Ceuta had no way of entering the Schengen area. In its response to the Spanish threat earlier on Friday, Italy's government said it would not accept "ultimatums". It added that it did not intend "under any circumstances to reconsider the decision to suspend the application of the Schengen Agreement for third-country nationals arriving from Spain, at least until August 15th and in any case until security and terrorist risks for Italy have been completely eliminated".Italian officials have said local authorities carrying out checks do "everything possible" to ensure maximum comfort for both Spanish and other European citizens arriving in Italy from Spain.Rome has also reiterated that Spanish citizens are exempt from additional checks when arriving in Italy, with these extra steps only for non-EU residents.However, El Pais reported that several airport terminals have seen long queues and waiting times in recent days, with passengers arriving from Spain directed to a specific line for checks.The counter-measures Madrid decided to impose on Friday would include passport, nationality and visa checks for Italian passengers and visitors from other countries arriving from Italy "amid the persistent irregular migratory pressure" the country was experiencing, a statement from Spain's government said.Checks would stay in place until 7 September "unless a change in the circumstances that led to its adoption warrants modifying that period". Temporary suspensions of the Schengen agreement are not unprecedented. Italy also maintains controls on its border with Slovenia.Italy's decision to suspend Schengen for a month was backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's membership to be temporarily suspended.Most of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta last week were returned within days. One hundred are believed to have died during the crossing. Nearly 1,400 minors, some of them "very young boys and girls", still remain there.Spain has not announced an anticipated second wave of crossings from Morocco. But BBC Arabic has found dozens of Facebook posts calling for a second crossing in mid-August, including some that advertised swimming equipment for sale. Six of these groups had more than 100,000 followers. Meta says it has removed posts that violate its policy.The Spanish prime minister's office told El Pais they were monitoring the situation but did not expect a repeat of scenes from last week.

schema.headline: Spain to impose border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies

title: Bristol Airport disruption a 'shambles' as flights restart
description: Anyone caught up in the disruption should contact their airline, they added. No further official information about the nature of the defect has been r
body: Anyone caught up in the disruption should contact their airline, they added. No further official information about the nature of the defect has been released. A number of people spoke to the BBC on Friday evening about their experience at the airport - among them Paul Smith, who was due to fly to Glasgow for his son's 20th birthday but had to cancel his trip."The communication, advice and support for passengers has been really poor," he said.There were no announcements on the tannoy system for over an hour, he said, which meant EasyJet reps in the departure lounge were the only source of information."What we've heard is that there's a hole in the runway."Dave Blackwell, travelling home from Rhodes in Greece, said it had been "a shambles" since his flight back to Bristol was diverted to Newcastle."We were in Rhodes Airport for three hours with no information. Now we have all been told our flight is going to Newcastle and then a five or six hour bus ride - why Newcastle? How appalling," he said.Are you waiting for a flight to or from Bristol Airport? title: Why have obesity rates doubled since 1993?
description: Obesity rates have doubled in England since 1993 - what's going on?Image source, Getty ImagesByJoe McFaddenHealth reporter and Hugh PymHealth editorIf
body: Obesity rates have doubled in England since 1993 - what's going on?Image source, Getty ImagesByJoe McFaddenHealth reporter and Hugh PymHealth editorIf England's obesity rates were still the same as 1993 there would be seven million fewer adults living with obesity.There are 14 million adults classified as obese, despite successive governments launching 14 separate obesity strategies over the past three decades.It's clear something isn't working, so what's behind the increase?And can anything be done about it?According to new analysis by the King's Fund, 15% of England's adult population - those aged 16 and over - in 1993 was obese, with rates achieving a record high of 30% in 2024.Their analysis suggests obesity rates are rising fastest in 16-to-24 year-olds, with 18% classified as obese or severely obese in 2024 compared with just 6% in 1993.Accounting for population change, this means there are now one million young adults living with obesity in England - 700,000 more than if rates had not risen over the past three decades.Dave Buck, senior fellow for public health at the King's Fund, called this rise "clearly worrying" and says governments have "talked the talk, but not sufficiently walked the walk" in addressing obesity rates."This analysis shows the scale of the failure to take the necessary action on tackling this obesity timebomb," he added.Why has obesity risen?There are several factors behind the rise in obesity, including changes in eating habits and food prices over the last 30 years.Service industry - or "white collar" jobs - take a larger share of the economy and there has been a decline in traditional manufacturing and other "blue collar" work such as manual labour.This means more people are in sedentary office jobs so spend more time sitting down than moving around.Food prices have also fallen since the 1990s, partly because of increased competition between the major supermarkets alongside an increase in fast food outlets and home delivery.Buck told the BBC that these changes mean it's "far easier to over-consume or consume in ways that add to our weight"."With things like deliveries, it's very easy and convenient now to click a button and you get a takeaway at your door, so we're making it much easier to have high fat, high salt and high sugar foods."Takeaways high in fats, salt and sugar are more widely available in areas of high deprivation where people are at higher risk of obesity.Less healthy foods in supermarkets are also cheaper than they were three decades ago, while there have been several cost-of-living crises in recent years.What has the government tried to do about it?Obesity can be a risk factor for several chronic conditions including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, osteoarthritis and some cancers.Reports estimate, external obesity and being overweight costs the UK economy approximately £126bn per year, including £12bn to the NHS - roughly 7% of its annual budget.Since 1992 - the year before data on obesity in England was first collected - 14 national obesity strategies have been published.Campaigners argue progress has been too slow and calls for further intervention have increased in recent years.Tony Blair's government introduced a ban on junk food advertising during children's TV programmes - although some campaigners were calling for a wider ban - while Gordon Brown launched a strategy aiming to reverse the "rising tide of obesity" after becoming prime minister in 2007.The Conservative government introduced a UK-wide levy on high-sugar soft drinks in 2018, causing several manufacturers to cut sugar levels in their products so that they fell below the levy threshold.During his final weeks in office in 2016, then-Prime Minister David Cameron considered banning "buy one get one free" deals for unhealthy products in supermarkets and restricting TV ads for junk food and other high sugar products.Although both Theresa May and Boris Johnson argued at times for further action, Cameron's ideas were not followed up, partly due to the pandemic which delayed plans further, and afterwards when ministers argued restrictions on such deals would be unfair on shoppers due to surging inflation.In January this year, the Labour government introduced a ban on junk food advertising before 21:00 on television and at any time online after almost a decade of consideration.Further plans to crack down on the sale of unhealthy food items are still yet to come into effect despite being first pledged by Labour in 2024, while a recent select committee report urged ministers to do more like stopping fast food outlets opening close to schools.What about weight loss drugs?Weight loss drugs such as GLP1s are increasingly being used to treat obesity, though only adults with a BMI of at least 35 and who have at least one pre-existing weight-related health condition qualify for Wegovy on the NHS.People with cardiovascular disease who are classed as overweight, but not quite obese, can also be given the drug, while Mounjaro has been available from specialist NHS weight-loss clinics in England and Wales since March 2025.Many people chose to buy these drugs privately.A new daily pill is already available in the US and could soon launch in the UK.The Department of Health and Social Care says weight loss jabs are only one part of a broader plan.It says tackling the promotion of less healthy food and drink, increasing exercise and encouraging people to eat healthier options are all important for addressing obesity.Earlier this year, England's Chief Medical Officer Prof Sir Chris Whitty said it would be a "societal failure" if medicating people for life was our only answer to obesity.He says the lessons are there in other countries, such as France, which have kept obesity levels stable.Now the question is what do we want to learn?Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?

schema.headline: Why have obesity rates doubled since 1993?

title: Liverpool transfers: Ronald Araujo close to season-long loan from Barcelona
description: Liverpool are close to signing Uruguay defender Ronald Araujo on a season-long loan from Barcelona.The deal includes an option to buy Araujo, who is e
body: Liverpool are close to signing Uruguay defender Ronald Araujo on a season-long loan from Barcelona.The deal includes an option to buy Araujo, who is expected to link up with the Liverpool squad this weekend.The 27-year-old centre-back has helped Barca win La Liga in three of the past four seasons, and ended last season as club captain.Araujo is under contract until 2031 but only made 11 league starts last season, with Gerard Martin and Pau Cubarsi emerging as their preferred central defensive pairing.After joining Barca from Uruguayan club Boston River in 2018, Araujo has made more than 200 appearances for the Spanish giants.Liverpool were looking to strengthen their defence after Ibrahima Konate left the Reds to join Real Madrid on a free transfer.

schema.headline: Liverpool transfers: Ronald Araujo close to season-long loan from Barcelona

title: Gloucestershire woman, 97, breaks record for oldest wingwalker
description: Figure caption, BySteve KnibbsGloucestershire and Clara BullockWest of EnglandA 97-year-old woman who suffered a stroke in 2025 has broken the Guinnes
body: Figure caption, BySteve KnibbsGloucestershire and Clara BullockWest of EnglandA 97-year-old woman who suffered a stroke in 2025 has broken the Guinness World Record for being the oldest female wing walker.Betty Bromage, who lives in Cheltenham, broke her own record which was set when she did the same challenge four years ago.Bromage raised funds for the stroke unit at Cheltenham General Hospital – where staff cared for her when she was sick.Speaking about having done six wing walks since the age of 87, she said: "I'd just get bored of life otherwise. I can't drive, I can't see very well and I get a bit frustrated. So, I want to do the things I can do."Image source, Betty BromageImage caption, Betty Bromage says she would be "bored" if she didn't do wingwalksIn August last year, Bromage had a stroke, which still affects her speech."They [the hospital] treated me so well. It affects my words but the rest of me is fine," she said.Image caption, Bromage broke her own record by completing the wingwalkShe added she raises money for charity because it can make a difference - and because she was inspired by some words she read on a hospital wall where she worked as a nurse."It said 'we pass through this world but once, any good we can do, any kindness we can show, do it now, do not defer or neglected, you will not pass this way again'," Bromage said.Image caption, Imogen Sims said it was "amazing" that Bromage was doing the challengeImogen Sims from Cheltenham and Gloucester Hospitals charity said staff were grateful Bromage is raising money for them."To take on such a daring challenge to support our team is amazing," Sims added."Donations will be used for equipment and will make a real difference for patients and staff."Bromage added: "The only problem is getting up on the wing because I'm quite short. Once you're up there, no problem. The fairground is a lot worse."I'll have to think of something when I'm 100 - something special."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Gloucestershire

schema.headline: Gloucestershire woman, 97, breaks record for oldest wingwalker

title: Chernobyl evacuee on Welsh family that took him in after disaster
description: Chernobyl disaster evacuee 'forever grateful' to Welsh family who took him inImage source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton Honchanka spent a month
body: Chernobyl disaster evacuee 'forever grateful' to Welsh family who took him inImage source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton Honchanka spent a month in Wales as part of the Chernobyl Lifeline programByOscar EdwardsBBC WalesUpdated 2 August 2026In the summer of 1999, 11-year-old Anton Honchanka was looking to escape his contaminated hometown following history's worst nuclear disaster.His journey would take him from Gomel, Belarus, to a United Kingdom that was experiencing a historic total solar eclipse, a major political reshuffle by Prime Minister Tony Blair, and a music chart dominated by singles such as Livin' La Vida Loca.Anton was one of the children evacuated from Belarus following the 1986 Chernobyl disaster in neighbouring Ukraine, after a reactor at the plant exploded and spewed out radioactive material that would spread across swathes of Europe.Due to radiation, parents in Eastern Europe saw the Chernobyl Children's Lifeline program (CCPL) as vital for their children's health with more than 56,000, external coming to the UK for medical aid and humanitarian support.Thirteen years on since the incident, and with the radiation still hanging in the air, Anton had set off on what he saw then as a "new adventure" thanks to the programme, albeit one "not easy" for his mum to see him leave."My mum was really happy that I had the opportunity to go on the trip," said Anton, now 38."But it wasn't easy for her not having me at home."Anton travelled by bus to Minsk, the capital of Belarus, and from there he flew to the UK.His first clear memory upon arriving in the UK was meeting his first host family. "That's where my experience in Wales really began," he said."My first impression was how peaceful and welcoming everything felt. It had such a cosy atmosphere that I felt comfortable almost straight away."Anton said the architecture was "different" from what he was used to in Belarus, with clean streets and a "warm and cosy atmosphere".His trip came at a time when Belarusian people were living in an increasingly authoritarian state, external, according to the UN Refugee Agency, in a period marked by severe political crackdowns and economic stagnation.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton, centre, stood with Dmitry on his left and the Amoss familyAnton and another boy called Dmitry spent the first two weeks with Angela Davies and her sons. Despite the language barrier, he said they all understood each other "perfectly".They were then taken to Llanharry, Rhondda Cynon Taf, to live with Peter and Linda Amoss.They welcomed the boys into their home with "incredible warmth", said Anton, finding ways to "spoil" and "surprise" them."They often took us shopping because they wanted to treat us," he said."They were always thinking about how they could make us smile."Anton said he naturally became great friends with their kids Gethin and Charlotte spending their time playing outside, riding bikes and enjoying their time together."Those are memories I'll always treasure," he added.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton visited landmarks such as St Fagans National Museum of HistoryFor Anton, returning home meant going "back to normal life" and he was surprised to find that "nothing had really changed".He and Dmitry gradually lost touch as they lived in different cities."When we arrived in Minsk, I got on a bus to Gomel, and he wasn't on it," he added.Now with two sons of his own, Honchanka said Wales and its people have "stayed in my heart forever"."I would really love to see my host families again if I have the opportunity.""During that time, they became very close and dear to me."Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton said they became his 'second family' during his time in WalesThis year marked 40 years since the Chernobyl nuclear disaster which caused a reactor to start spewing out radioactive material that would spread across swathes of Europe.Children from Belarus and Ukraine stayed with host families for four-week recuperative breaks. The clean air, untainted food and clean water helped to lower the levels of caesium and other radiation stored in the children's bodies.Gerrie Bayley, 74, from Prestatyn, first joined the CPPL in 2004 taking in two girls from Belarus.She enjoyed the experience so much, it has since "become her life" and she now serves as the chair of the charity's north Wales branch.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Dmitry, in the Liverpool shirt, lost contact with Anton when they returned to BelarusGerrie said the few weeks in the UK made a remarkable difference to their health."They would sleep all the time. They had these big black circles under their eyes. "By the end of the month, they had energy and were eating well. I cannot say how much difference it made."The communities rallied around the program providing second-hand clothing, free dentist appointments and eye tests for the children."They all had treatment they needed. So many stores helped out." she said.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton became great friends with the Amoss kids during his stayLinda Amoss, 71, said the family were vetted to make sure they had a spare bedroom with enough capacity to house Anton and Dmitry"As far as they were concerned we were a second family."They had already been in the country for a couple of weeks and we were the second family for the latter two weeks of their stay."Linda said she was told that any time spent outside of Belarus would "benefit their health"."There were children with incredibly high rates of cancer in certain areas," she added.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton has two sons of his own called Dmitry and DemyanLike Anton, she said the language was something they had to overcome, but it ultimately proved no issue as the boys "just clicked in"."Food was sometimes a bit of an issue, but my cooking isn't the best anyway," she added.Anton joined the family on trips to local landmarks such as St Fagans, Oakwood Theme Park and Garth Hill. "I don't remember them being particularly homesick because everything was sort of just so new and bright for them," said Linda.Image source, Linda AmossImage caption, Peter and Linda Amoss looked after Anton for two weeks during his stay As the four weeks drew to a close, Linda said she understood that the chance of the boys being able to return to the UK was "very slim" due to the demand for places in Ukraine and Belarus.Until now, she had not heard from Anton or Dmitry, but said it would be "extremely brilliant" if they could meet in person again.She also takes great pride in Wales' role in the Chernobyl Children's Lifeline programme."Wales is incredibly hospitable, and I really do love that about our country," she added.

schema.headline: Chernobyl evacuee on Welsh family that took him in after disaster
